utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll move into private session to deal with two matters. It will not take very long.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I know that the Prosecution had two short preliminary matters, but I invite them to postpone that until later. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. And, meanwhile, I'll deal with document D557, which was MFI'd during the testimony of Nenad Kecmanovic. A few pages of D555 -- 557, I apologise, which is a 77-page document, entitled "Islamic Declaration," was used with Witness Kecmanovic. In September the Defence advised the Chamber that it would seek to tender the entire document. On the 13th of October of this year, the Chamber requested the Defence to file submissions giving the reasons as to why the entire document should be admitted. The Chamber hereby sets a deadline of the 19th of December, 2014, for these submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Amidzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President of the Trial Chamber. Good morning, Your Honours, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Amidzic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up in e-court Exhibit D847, which should be the statement of the witness. And could we please turn to page 6 of the same in both languages. I apologise. It will be one page prior in the English. We're looking at paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph you mention that you provided three sets of field kitchen trailers for the Nepalese Battalion of the UN forces. Can you tell us how and why it came to be that you were called upon to provide these to the Nepalese Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Judges, in response to this question, I'm going to say the following. We kept this buffer zone in Slavonia; or rather, the units of my corps that separated the warring peoples and disabled conflicts, although conflicts were under way. As this area was left, according to the agreement reached between the JNA and UNPROFOR it was the peacekeeping forces that took over, or rather the forces, for ensuring that area. That was the Nepalese and Argentinian Battalions. When this area was taken and when this function was taken over from our units, I was asked for three kitchens with tents and equipment for preparing meals in the field. My organs gave this to them, and they were supposed to give it back, which, indeed, they did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just get some clarification, Witness. You are recorded as having said "disabled conflicts." This is at page 4, line 13. Was it disabled conflicts? It doesn't make sense what -- that you said. Or is it disabled convicts? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me read the sentence to you. You say: "We kept this buffer zone in Slavonia; or rather, the units of my corps that separated the warring peoples and disabled conflicts..." Or are you -- is the disabled -- is a vapier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my language that is what it means, to disable conflicts, not to make conflicts possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd now to now look at paragraph number 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which should be on the next page in both languages of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here it says that prisoners of war organised the preparation and distribution of their own food at Manjaca. Can you please explain for us the manner how food was provided for them to prepare and distribute themselves.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That task, as well as the task in general that was being carried out for all combat units in terms of working along these patterns, as we say, we carried this out through the organs that were the mainstays of these activities. However, the command of the camp provided the numbers and the requests to the Kozara barracks and then they made calculations according to standards and then provided food and other things to the camp. It is true that the prisoners themselves organised the preparation and distribution of food. My duty was also not only to provide food but also accommodation, change of clothing, and bathing. I can add another thing. The assortment of articles and needs that were provided according to these calculations did not differ at all from the rations I provided to others. Often this was not sufficient, but that was the case for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have just said: "The assortment of articles and needs that were provided according to these calculations did not differ at all from the rations I provided to others." What "others" are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean other units that were there for security in the entire area, because the POW camp had to be supplied with food according to the norms and standards that are prescribed otherwise. I made no distinction between the members of the army and the persons who were in the camp. I did it in an equal way, depending on the numbers involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at paragraph 37 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the quantity of food needed was calculated and that you made no distinction between security and the prisoners of war. Were you there when the food was distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most often I was not because the POWs organised this themselves. As for inspections, I could not adjust it to that, and it was a rare occasion when I would be there when food was being distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So -- so whether -- I do understand that there was not sufficient food. What -- what quantity was -- was it 50 per cent? What was needed that was provided? Or 70 per cent or -- could you tell us a bit more about that? On average.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you about percentages. The assortment of articles differed. Sometimes there was a full assortment, and sometimes certain articles were lacking. So when I didn't have that, I didn't have it for others either when I had no way of getting ahold of things like that. I'm saying that the pattern of supply was the same for officers and soldiers and on the front and these persons who were in the POW camp. In the same way, the rules were being applied. The rules governing supplies. It depended on what I had. At certain points I had more and then, say, the following day I would have less. Often the meals would simply be poorer. There wouldn't be a full assortment of articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how could you be sure that those who were providing security would, in effect, get the same poor rations and not - which one could imagine - either take more than their share was or take less than their share was. How would you know who finally got what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ultimately that is really difficult to be everywhere, because it's a big area, a large number of units, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I do understand that you finally would not, could not know for certain whether it was shared in the way as it was calculated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the contrary. My calculations, yes, and everyone in the field got whatever was possible. And my organs did that in a very professional and responsible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said it's really difficult to be everywhere which means that you finally were not able to verify whether it all went as it was planned and as it was calculated who really got what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge, sir, the commander of the unit is the one that counts, and then they can give me information saying there wasn't sufficient and so on. However, I sent people of my own to check, and then we would improve the situation as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To check what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything. Rules, standards, application, quality of meals, way of distribution, cleanliness, hygiene, everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did your people find that needed to be improved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite a bit. There is a broad spectrum in terms of all the objections that we heard, and it depended on the people who would use the articles they received. Also hygiene. Were they prepared, ready to do that. Also cleanliness, personal cleanliness, clothing, and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have preferred to have concrete answers rather than general statements, but I leave it to that. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one follow up question. You said, Witness, you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, sir, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Please, we are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Listen to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not used to being interrupted. Please proceed, Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us that the prisoners of war did the preparation and distribution of the food by themselves. How did they organise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a particular point where the kitchen was for cooking. Then there was a particular area with certain tables for distribution. And then there was a certain lineup. I mean, in terms of the way how these persons who were in camp were brought. Then after the cooking, the commander of the camp had to be present to taste the food and to approve its distribution. That was the sign that the food was prepared in a proper way, that it was healthy, and that it could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: However, you didn't tell me how the prisoners of war organised themselves. This was the question. Because earlier you said they organised it by their own. How did they do that? I'm not asking about the commander and about his duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. On the basis of mutual -- I mean, selection or the command -- on the basis of the composition involved, I mean, the persons who were found there, who were professional waiters, who could do that kind of work, they were involved in such obligations and then they would do that for the entire camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the prisoners decided who is a professional waiter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, don't forget that when persons came in and were processed, that was very detailed. During that processing and during that registration, the command and the persons who comprised the security of the camp have an exact overview of the structure of these persons and also what they could be involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you didn't answer my question how the prisoners organised themselves. But I leave it to that. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything additional to tell the Judges, or can we move on, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should explain yet again. In every respect in terms of regulations that camp was well organised. From the moment those people entered and were processed, there was no doubt that they could have been engaged in the organisation of work in the camp itself. As for the camp administration or the camp command, they knew exactly who they could engage and who they couldn't, because they were not capable of working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I'd like to turn to the next page in your statement and look at paragraph 37. Here, sir, you're explaining that since you were at your maximum, you allowed and humanitarian organisations provided additional materials to provide a higher standard of life to those in Manjaca camp. Can you identify for us which humanitarian aid organisations these were that did this.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this part of the answer is the addition to my previous answer. There were shortages and there were gaps in security, and I therefore allowed humanitarian organisations to fill the gaps and to provide for what I could not provide. Those same representatives of humanitarian organisations inspected the camp so we could together ascertain what needed to be brought in, equipment, cleaning agents, personal hygiene articles, and food I could not provide. To be more specific, most commonly they brought in medicines and a whole range of necessities in terms of medical supplies. And as for their names, most commonly, it was Merhamet, the Muslim charitable organisation headquartered in Banja Luka, and Caritas, also a charitable organisation run by the Catholic church. The Red Cross, the local Red Cross was also present, and you already know about the role that the International Red Cross played in all that. I apologise. I told all of them there and then what my capabilities were and I welcomed them all. As far as I know, they inspected the area even without me. When they were announced they were allowed to get in. I am not aware of the fact that any of their announced visits was not approved. All those who could play a role and improve the standard of living and the humanitarian situation of those who were kept in the camp were more than welcome to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at paragraph 39, the same page in English, the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you mention that you read reports and found statements, even of those that visited the Manjaca with you, with meant -- misrepresentations about Manjaca. Can you tell us what reports or statements you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really need to start my answer to this question in this way, in the following way: All those who escorted me very often and what I established during my controls did not reflect the situation as was portrayed by the persons who were often visiting the camp with me. We looked at the same things and then their stories ended up being different. They would end up saying that a lot of irregular things were going on, including inhumane treatment, ill-treatment, torture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. I'm also addressing you, Mr. Ivetic. You were asked what statements you were talking about. Of course you'll understand, Mr. Ivetic, that this Chamber is unable to evaluate any evidence which says some statements I heard or that and that without knowing what statements we are talking about. Apart from that, it's not usual for a witness who tells us that he was often not present, that he could tell us exactly that those who are telling about certain events are not telling the truth where the witness himself apparently, or we could check that on the basis of the statements he's talking about, whether he was present or not, whether he went -- can contradict that. And by the way, it's not a matter of telling that someone else is not telling the truth. But if this witness has any specific knowledge about certain events, we'd like to hear that. And then, of course, we have to evaluate and we have to assess which is the truth, what is the truth, and what is not. But these kind of sweeping general statements of others not telling the truth doesn't assist the Chamber. Could you please be focused in your questions on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought I was by asking what statements he's talking about, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- you were, but then you let the witness just go and he says before answering the question I have to make all kind of statements. You could have reminded him at that moment that you require him to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please identify for us precisely what statements you are referring to in this paragraph of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I was preparing for this testimony, I came across the statements of the witnesses who testified here before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, that's an answer to the question. I take it that you then refer to those statements and that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apparently studied them. Who provided them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was preparing myself for this testimony, I came across a statement by Colonel Selak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you at this moment whose statement you were talking about. Who provided the statement to you or how did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was being provided with materials from -- by the Defence team and when I wanted to be acquainted with all the materials in order to prepare for this appearance. A lot of the things were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple answer is: They were given to me by the Defence. Because that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you tell us exactly what you received from the Defence, names of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that statement that I am trying to interpret and use here in order to provide my own explanation. Again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I stop you. My question was: Whose statements you received by the Defence. So I expect you to tell me Witness A, Witness B, Witness -- I just want names at this moment so that we know what statements you received and reviewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the specific case, Colonel Osman Selak. His statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you receive any other statement, and did you review any other statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have an opportunity. However, I saw parts of his statement where it says exactly this. I don't know what was happening there. I don't know. But people told me, people from Merhamet told me that. That's what I saw in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand that the only statement you have read and reviewed was the statement of Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then give us the name of the other witnesses whose statements you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist. There's a translation issue. He said [Interpretation] "he has several statements," referring to Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine, if you have several statements. Whose statements do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. His statements, Osman Selak's statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have statements of any other witness, other than Selak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this matter, apart from Selak's, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What do you have from Selak's statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I've just told you. In one part of his statement, it says as follows: When it comes to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll come to that later. I first want to know: Do you have one statement of Selak, do you have several statements of Selak? And, if so, how many.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't be sure how many. However, one of them deals with this issue and I remember very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, I can't remember what year that statement was from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no. I want you first to answer my questions. You want to move through a certain subject and we need information before we come to that subject. If there's any specific matter -- Mr. Mladic, are you supposed to remain seated, first of all. If there's any translation issue, Mr. Stojanovic, tell us. Apparently there is a ... is there no audio? No loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told everything should be okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I want you -- we want to know exactly on what your statement in this respect is based, and that's the reason why we want to have that information first. What you did see? How many pages? Was it a short statement? Was it a long statement? How many statements have you seen? From Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several statements on several occasions. They were all by Selak. But what he dealt with in this particular statement, I remember that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, we'll come to that. Please answer my questions first. You say you have seen -- are they all short statements, and in what language are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those statements were in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how was that -- did you also read transcripts of the testimony of Mr. Selak or did you just read statements which he signed like the statement you've given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't make a distinction between the two. I think it was a transcript. I don't know what you mean when you say "the transcript of his statement." It was the transcript -- transcript of his testimony or statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What a statement is is the relatively short report of an interview in which you just see what the person may have said. Like your statement as you find it on your screen now. That's what I call a statement. What I call a transcript is a verbatim record of what someone tells us in court, which means that you'll see question put, answers, interventions saying we take a break, et cetera, et cetera. Now, what you did you -- and usually those transcripts are relatively long. That is, could be easily 30, 40, 50, 60 pages, whereas usually statements are short; that is, anything between two and often not more than ten pages. What did you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just told you, a transcript. It was longer than a statement that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that was in what language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this Chamber is not aware of any transcript being prepared -- although there is a translation problem at this moment. Mr. Ivetic, could you tell us out as to whether -- And let me ask you first: Where did you get that transcript from? Did you get it from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've told you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ivetic, were any which is possible transcript provided to the witness in preparing for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic prepared this witness and my understanding is that only ICTY statements were -- would have been given to the witness to comment upon if he knew anything about specific allegations of Mr. Selak, and it is possible that a Google translation of the draft statement was also provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it's at this moment, if I could say so, it's more likely than not that he was provided with an English or at least a -- statements taken in B/C/S or written down in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My understanding is all the ICTY statements are taken in English with a B/C/S translation provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But statements, not testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I've also indicated that I believe also a Google translation of the transcript could also be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. All right. Now, when this witness makes this statement about I heard, I was told, et cetera, I may take it that when he was interviewed that it was verified what he exactly referred to rather than putting on paper any comment without having verified on what it was based? What it referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the witness has five times today tried to identify particularly the statement from Mr. Selak, the particular words of Mr. Selak that he's been referencing, and you have not permitted him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're invited to clarify this issue in the way I did it because I do understand that I do it not as you consider it to be appropriately done. Please be aware that the statement, as it is now, lacks sufficient basis, and you're invited to clarify this viva voce because you are claiming, if I understand you well, that you better know how to do that and I gladly accept that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do not know better than you, Your Honour. You have asked questions and the witness has started to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I said that you may proceed. Would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would, Your Honours, and I would also direct Your Honours to paragraphs 64 through 68 of the statement that deal particularly with Mr. Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, could you please answer what the Judge did not let you answer: What particular parts of Mr. Selak's statement are you referencing in your discussion in paragraphs 39 and 40?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I didn't make a distinction. I really don't know the distinction between a transcript and a statement. It probably will be a statement. But what am I talking about? In that statement by Osman Selak, I found a part where he describes the situation in the prisoner of war camp at Manjaca. He says that there was inhumane treatment, ill-treatment, and even killings of prisoners. He says: I don't know, but I was told that by people from Merhamet. He continues to say that in that camp, according to them, about 40 people were killed. I referred to that part of the statement and I provide my answer accordingly. I did not make up anything. I did not add anything. Your Honours, I was surprised for that person to say some 40. In our language 40 is 40, and some 40 could be 39 or 41 or any other unspecified number of people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, do you think "some 40" could also be 18 or 65, or would be it be, well, let's say, anywhere between 35 and 45?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my problem exactly, Your Honour. When he says "some 40," he means around 40. I really can't tell you with certainty whether it is anything between 35 and 45. It is a very non-specific piece of information which cannot be pin-pointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said "or any other unspecified number," which would range from whatever, whereas I understand "some 40" to mean in the range of approximately 40, that would be at least anywhere between 30 and 50, but I asked you this because you said it could be any unspecified number which is a far wider range than the one I put to you, as my understanding of what "some 40" means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you sincerely, Your Honour, I don't know what he meant. This is just my objection. This is an important piece of information and still he presents it in a very non-specified way. He may have had in mind 39 or 41, he is not sure about this figure, 40. Still, it's a very important piece of information and to tackle with such recklessness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, Mr. Ivetic, as I said before, if the witness can tell us anything specific which contradicts or supports or -- about the same events, we'd like to hear. But to -- for the witness to tell us what is appropriately accepted into evidence or not may not be the most important thing to hear from a witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to page 9 in English and page 10 in Serbian, and we should then be looking at paragraphs 44 through 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you describe bringing an ICRC and international humanitarian representative delegation to the Mali Novi Logor barracks to show them that this was not a prisoner of war camp. First of all, who if anyone came with you and these officials to the barracks on this occasions?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the Banja Luka garrison, there is and there was the Mali and Novi Logor barracks, Logor meaning a camp. And there was an association with the war camps. In the Mali Novi Logor there was a military investigation prison where military personnel was kept while they were waiting to be tried or investigated. That facility was a military prison or a detention unit. I inspected it with General Mladic with representatives of the International Red Cross with our host from the barracks who was responsible for the control and care of that facility. We showed everybody everything. We opened all the rooms and as we were passing through the facility, we also had brief conversations with the people who were kept there. We entered everything single room, we saw every single person, we controlled the corridor, and finally we opened the area in -- below the staircase where brooms were kept in a little closest just to show everybody that we were not hiding anything. The representatives of the Red Cross and some other people who were there, and I don't know which organisation they belonged to, did not have anything to say to everything that they had seen. They did not have any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we get a date for this visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the year or date or time of year for this visit to the Mali Novi Logor barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would not want to speculate, but it was in the month of August 1993. I think it was on the 27th of August or during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at paragraph 46 on the same page. Here you talk of the Croat population running from Muslim forces in Central Bosnia. Can you be a bit more specific precisely what region these Croats were coming from? What is the name for that region?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, the answer to this question goes as this. I received a task from my superior command, it was signed by Mr. Mladic. It was to receive the population from Central Bosnia who were threatened and more specifically from the Lasva valley around the town of Travnik. Am I making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If I --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population that was threatened and members of the Croatian Defence Council were simply fleeing before Muslim forces and they were seeking refuge in our territory. That was approved. And then we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can interrupt. If I can interrupt, we do have some of that in your statement. I have two more questions I'd like to get to hopefully before we take the first break. Sir, in paragraph 49 on the next page in English and page 10 in the Serbian, you talk about HVO members that surrendered their weapons and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should not speak at an audible volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and were temporarily accommodated in Manjaca. How long did they stay in Manjaca and where did they go after?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, members of the HVO, around 300 of them, decided to surrender. They their own lists. They surrendered their weapons. With their consent they were taken to facilities of the former camp, and at that moment it was no longer a camp and they did not have the status as prisoners of war. They stayed there not more than ten days, and during that time the further procedure was organised. Upon the order of our superior command, we used lorries with tarpaulin to transport them to the area of Vares. They had to move across our territory, and those who wanted to go to Ilijas and Sarajevo, we could not meet that request because those areas were under the control of Muslim forces, so they faced further problems there if they had been sent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I'd like to look on the same page in English and the next page in Serbian, and my last question deals with paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the next -- pardon me. We should go to page 12 in the English and page 12 in -- page 13 in Serbian. And paragraph number 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you say about General Mladic: "All that I heard and pictured about him earlier was proven right about his personality when I was on an official visit to the Knin Corps." What precisely had you heard and pictured about General Mladic which was proven true and from whom had you heard it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the regular visit to the Knin Corps with my previous commander, with a view to an exchange of experience, I spoke to the assistant commander for morale of that corps whose name was Mesud Hasotic. He was a colonel and he was assistant commander for morale for that corps. Since I did not know the name or surname of the head of the quartermaster's division, and that is what I was interested in, he took me to the chief whose name was Ibro. I could remember his last name. He was a colonel, too. We talked about all sorts of things, and they told me about Mr. Ratko Mladic who was then Chief of Staff of that corps who was a real soldier's man, a man's man who asked for discipline and order and all on the basis of the personal example that he set. As a soldier, I recognised my own attitude and fitting into requirements, although I didn't know that he would be my commander in the coming period too. May I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could also tell us the ethnicity of Mr. Mesud Hasotic and Ibro while continuing.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mesud Hasotic is a Muslim. He still lives in Banja Luka. And Colonel Ibro, as I've already said I cannot remember his last name, he is also a Muslim, but I don't know where he hails from and where he lives right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And have you completed your description of how they described General Mladic to you as you later found to be proven right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. The first time I met General Mladic, that was the day of the assembly when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, when the Main Staff was established, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and when he was appointed commander of that staff. I met him in front of the hall and at first sight all of this was confirmed and a lot more than that; namely, he that is very resolute, energetic, and above all he showed this decisiveness and this fairness by his own example. I was really inspired by that. And later on we would see each other as we carried out our tasks, either when I went to report to him in the Main Staff or he would come to me command. We did such a lot of work together. And never, really, he never disappointed me. I had great confidence in him. We did so many things together and I saw that he had confidence in me too and that he appreciated what I did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of the Defence team, I thank you for answering my questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination and I see we're -- I thank the translators for the indulgence of the extra five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I recognise the time. I have one question for the Defence for the record before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need the witness for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't need the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we would first -- I would have one question for you, Witness. You told us about your role in the -- to provide food and all kind of facilities for the Manjaca prisoners of war camp. Could you tell us exactly until when you performed that duty? I mean, on -- when did that stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement, Mr. President of the Trial Chamber, it says exactly the 14th of February, 1993, when I took over another duty. It was 1993. It was 1993. Yes, sorry. And then Colonel Bulic took over from me. And this was after the Serbian new year. It's written in the statement. I don't like to guess as far as dates are concerned. I am afraid that I may make a mistake and then it may turn out to be on purpose when it's not, and you really have it in the statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness. Mr. Ivetic, could you help me exactly where if I find it? And I don't know whether it's phrased in a similar way as I asked or whether I should conclude that from other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The 14th of February 1993 date is in paragraph 2 of the statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 2. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When he was appointed assistant commander for logistics on 14th February 1993. In relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now understand that I have to understand that change in position as the point in time. Are -- you are saying that when you were appointed assistant commander for logistics, which was on the 14th of February, 1993, that your duties in relation to providing food -- well, whatever, to Manjaca ended. Then one more question. Did your successor take over that responsibility or was it ended anyhow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, security for that specific POW camp did not function then because the camp did not function either. It had been disbanded on -- I mean, in November of the previous year. So there was no need. But, Mr. President, at any rate he did all of this work or he would have done all this had it been necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you have answered my question. We'll take a break. We'd like to see you back at 11.00. And you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, paragraph 38 [Realtime transcript read in error "30"] has the date of the closure of Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, it's paragraph 38. I see paragraph 30 in the transcript. I may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- I have to combine the information so as to find the -- an answer to my question. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The one very brief matter, I just was going to request that the Defence confirm or correct, whichever is appropriate, my understanding that the witness was provided statements by another witness which are not in evidence before this Trial Chamber and that some of his comments on those witness's statements relate to material that's not in evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll have to check during the break and I will endeavour to come back with a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I can tell you that one of the things I also did over the last half an hour was to try to find specific references to 40 prisoners being killed. I looked at the transcript. I had difficulties until now in finding it. I have not started looking at 15 people from the city prison yet. But since the witness comments apparently on statements of what he now tells us Mr. Selak, the Chamber also would very much appreciate to know where that -- to find in any material which was admitted into evidence. Because if it's not in evidence, then of course we should not pay attention to it because we're unavailable to verify the basis of it. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for the witness to come in, I can give some additional information that I've been able to obtain through my preliminary inquiries in the back. The Serbian language transcript of the witness mentioned was the transcript of proceedings from the Tadic case from transcript pages 1221 through 1305 of that proceeding because that transcript was available in the Serbian language and was then provided to the witness. In addition, I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not in evidence, I think. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. It's not in evidence. I apologise if I did not make that clear. And the -- in terms of what is in evidence, we have a -- excerpts from Osman Selak's diary, which is P253. We have the OTP witness statement of Osman Selak, which is P244. We have also a letter written by Osman Selak, which is D53. And there's some kind of chart that may have comments that were by Mr. Selak. I'm not sure whether that was provided to the witness or not. That is P259. And there's -- I mention these are additional statements of Mr. Selak that were not in evidence, and my staff is assisting to specify those by either ERN number or by date so that I can report back to you with that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And were you able to find the specific references to the 40 and the 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have not. I'm going to continue to do that while in the courtroom while Mr. Traldi begins his cross to try to assist both the Chamber and the Prosecution in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to briefly respond, not just the 40 and the 15 but the material discussed in paragraph 64 through I believe it's 68 of the statement would be relevant and might affect some of the choices I make during cross-examination. As to P259 that Mr. Ivetic mentioned, just for the clarity of the record those were comments that were made by the witness on documents that he reviewed in preparation for his testimony in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having clarified this, Mr. Traldi, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent not limited by what we discussed earlier. Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. And may I ask you to very much focus on the question. If there's anything to be added wait for follow-up questions, and if at the very end something needs to be added you will have an opportunity to do so. But start by answering the questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to start with some questions about the structure of the 1st Krajina Corps. You say in paragraph 10 of your statement, now Exhibit D847, and I'm providing the reference for the record, I have a very simply question. You say that primary command post was in Banja Luka. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call that the primary command post. It is in building of the former command, otherwise in the centre of the town of Banja Luka. Whoever is familiar with that area will know that we did not change that. And then depending on operations and tasks, this was in the function of the forward command post too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, at this point and I'd ask you to focus very closely on the question. I'd asked you only about the primary command post, or what you describe as the primary command post. When you say "it is in the building of the former command," you're referring to the former command of the 5th Corps of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What was that building called?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll move on then. You mention a forward command post was established in Prnjavor in your statement. That forward command post was established in the middle of June 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Further on, from June onwards it was in Prnjavor, the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention in paragraph 10 of D847 that the commander and the Chief of Staff of the 1st Krajina Corps were at that forward command post in Prnjavor. That refers to General Momir Talic and General Bosko Kelecevic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, even during the period when they were based in Prnjavor, General Talic and General Kelecevic would sometimes come back to Banja Luka for meetings or to carry out command responsibilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a rule, but most often reporting would take place where they were, and they would come, in connection with important tasks and activities, to Banja Luka for these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When they came to Banja Luka, would they ever come to the Kozara barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that question to be unclear, not defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When General Talic and General Kelecevic came to Banja Luka during the period of the war, would they ever visit the Kozara barracks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I asked to be defined. They could go there on a task because there were units there that were subordinated. And the buildings where these units were, if necessary they could visit, but I cannot say how often and when. At any rate, they came to the building of the command where I was too because of their own business that they had to carry out and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was whether they ever went to that barracks when visiting. I do understand from your answer that they did. Yes, that would have been the simple answer. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned they also visited the building that you were based in. What building was that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely this building of the command of the 5th Corps. I don't see what you're asking me. You're asking me for a name, and I don't know what the name of that might have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know the street address of this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the street next to it is called Prvi Krajiski Korpus, and it is perpendicular to this street, this lane, of the former JNA. Well, I never received mail on that address, so I cannot say on the basis of this postal address. I received mail at the military post code and I was there for ten years and even more, and now I cannot tell you the address just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, sir. Thank you. You don't know the street address. Thank you, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were based in this building as chief of the quartermaster service. Was the logistics organ of the 1st Krajina Corps based in this building?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, the logistics organ and the command of the logistics base. And some other organs, I mean, that were there, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered the question. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So Colonel Tepsic was also based in this building at the beginning of the war; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned the commands of the logistics base. Colonel Selak was also based in this building at the beginning the war then; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And after he left in July, Colonel Skondric would have been based in the same building as you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were any of the other organs of the 1st Krajina Corps command based in that building? And I'm referring specifically to the security and intelligence organ, the legal morale and religious affairs organ, the civilian affairs organ, or any other organs you may want to discuss.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for those that were the forward command post, all of those who were from the command of the 1st Corps were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned it's on Prvi Krajiski Korpus Street. That's 1st Krajina Corps Street; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it is called that. I mean, the street that is on the western side. That one is what I know for sure. But as for the rest that you ask me about, I cannot say that with certainty because I don't know street names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall what street was called before the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're asking me something that I cannot remember, yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to your responsibilities as chief of the quartermaster service in the 1st Krajina Corps. From whom would you directly receive your tasks when you were chief of the quartermaster service?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a disciplinary and organisational point of view, from Colonel Tepsic, the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did General Talic ever task you directly or were you always tasked through Colonel Tepsic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost always and always through my immediate superior who was his assistant commander, Colonel Tepsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To whom would you report on your work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you please seek clarification of "almost always and always," which I have some difficulties to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, did you mean to say you were always tasked through Colonel Tepsic, your immediate superior, or almost always tasked but sometimes tasked directly by other people?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Colonel Tepsic. But I wouldn't be surprised if I were to find a document here that had to do with my professional line of work containing an order that was issued by my second superior officer. Although, I cannot say Karic. It would be Tepsic always.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would you also report on your work to Colonel Tepsic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He received his taskings and reported on his work from General Talic, the corps commander; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Aside from the quartermaster service, the logistics service also had a technical service; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the beginning of May 1992, the chief of the technical service was Colonel Muharem Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Muharem Talic? I don't think that would be the last name. Check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall the gentleman's last name?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall. But I don't think that it's the same last name as my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's have 65 ter 16612, please, and we can check my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, in June 1992, the chief of the technical service became Lieutenant-Colonel Dragoljub Jankovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the signature here. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is the note handing over duty or reflecting the hand-over of duty from Colonel Muharem Talic to Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for the possibility that I was wrong when I said what I said. I really don't remember that that was his last name. We communicated on a first-name basis and that is how we addressed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This gentleman you called Muharem, what was his ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Colonel Dragoljub Jankovic was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He had a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 16612.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16612 receives exhibit number P6986, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In 1993 when you became assistant commander for logistics, you would then receive your tasks from General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was his assistant commander, and I received my tasks from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you would report on your work to him; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I to him, and the chiefs to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is Muharem Talic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is -- just for clarity, I'm referring to General Momir Talic, the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was that how you understood me, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you were assistant commander for logistics, you would receive information about upcoming operations from the corps commander, General Talic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the collegium and with the commander, we always examined such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And based on the information you received, you would assess logistical needs of the units which would be carrying those operations out; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. On the basis of their reports and requests, we would not assess that. We would have cumulatively the needs of all, and then we would apply ourselves to the meeting of these needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You'd do that by assigning subordinate logistical units to fill those needs; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not assign them within my --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the answer. Come closer to the microphone and speak distinctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness you're invited to come a bit closer to the microphone to repeat your answer. You started by saying, I did not assign them within ... and could you then repeat from what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman asked me whether I gave assignments to someone. The 14th Logistics Base was the mainstay of my activity, and I would submit my needs to them for realisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to look at just one example, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 18346.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is coming from the 5th Corps, it's dated the 9th of May, 1992, signed by your superior Colonel Tepsic. So it's before the transformation.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We read here: "On the basis of demonstrated need, and with the goal of raising the level of combat readiness of the Territorial Defence units, pursuant to a verbal order by the commander of the 5th Corps." And then we see that Colonel Tepsic is ordering the distribution to the Kotor Varos Municipal Territorial Defence Staff of a number of weapons and other supplies. This is how the provision of logistical resources to subordinated forces is supposed to work as a standard matter in the JNA and the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the best example, but in principle this is one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18346 receives exhibit number P6987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6987 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to the meetings of the corps commander that you mention in your statement. You refer to a regular meeting at 0715 hours in the morning. Where was that meeting held, as of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer you by saying that I don't know. From May 1992 onwards, I was not in that role, and I did not take part in the role of my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you began attending that meeting in February 1993; right? The commanders' morning meeting.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did the assistant commanders of security and intelligence, legal, morale, and religious affairs, and civilian affairs also attend the commanders' morning meeting at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle they did, and they were supposed to be there. If you are mentioning what happened before my take-over of duty, I don't know, but afterwards they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at that point, the assistant commander for civilian affairs was Gojko Vujinovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security and intelligence was Colonel Bogojevic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogojevic Stevan, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the assistant commander for legal, morale, religious affairs was Milutin Vukelic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I'm not sure if all names are correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One has just been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Colonel Bogojevic's last name, that's spelled B-o-g-o-j-e-v-i-c; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Are you asking me? Yes. As far as I know his name is Stevan, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: General Talic ran these meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always the corps commander. In his absence when he was prevented from attending, it would be the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that was General Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would he also attend the meetings even when General Talic was there and running them?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And General Talic, or General Kelecevic if he was replacing him, could hand out tasks at these meetings; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that would be correct. Because that was briefing. Issues were discussed and tasks were handed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "issues were discussed," would the different sectors report on the work they'd been doing?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every chief of sector submitted a report on the work of his sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to shift now to a different type of meeting. You mentioned a moment ago a group called the corps commanders' collegium that I understand met weekly. Aside from the chiefs of sector that you mentioned a moment ago, who else would attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it was an inner circle: The commander, the Chief of Staff, and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did the head of the 14th Logistics Base also attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he was not the commander of the 14th Logistics Base and he was not a member of the 1st or the 5th Corps. He was never duty-bound do attend those meetings, nor he did. The commander could have invited him when he considered some common issues or when he had the time to give him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, could we have paragraph 66 of D847 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, when you said he was not the commander, who did you have on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not understand me. He was the commander of the 14th Logistics Base but he was not an organic member of the corps. He was subordinated to his superior command as the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, you're invited to slow down. But it's still not clear to me whether he was or was not. But who did you have on your mind when you said, as you now clarified, was the commander of the 14th Logistics Base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the commander of the 14th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 66 of your statement here, and can you see it on the screen, you say: "As the commander of the base, he was obliged to attend the weekly meetings of the corps commander's collegium... " That's the statement that you reviewed, made corrections to, and swore was truthful. Do you stand by what you've said here in paragraph 66 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a misinterpretation. He could attend. He should have attended once a week. But not at the time when the commander discussed issues with his immediate subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have invited him at any other moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I asked you would the commander of the logistics base attend the collegium. You said back at transcript page 41, line 15, he was never duty-bound to attend those meetings. You say, in paragraph 66, the commander of the logistics base was obliged to attend the weekly meetings. So I'm not asking you about what issues were discussed at what time. I am asking you now, having said in your statement that the commander of the logistics base was obliged to attend and then said in your testimony that he was not, which of those answers you stand by, whether the commander of the logistics base was or was not obliged to attend the weekly meeting of the corps commander's collegium.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the collegium meetings, they were chaired by the commander. The questions and issues that he dealt with together with the commander of the logistics base, he found time with the collegium or without the collegium in the way and according to the nature of the tasks that he had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, to which you attested, you say that the commander of the base was obliged to attend these meetings. Today in your testimony, you told us that he was not obliged. Which of the two is your evidence now today, which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the commander invited those who were not on the collegium, they had to attend. They did not have to attend all the collegium meetings organised by the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he was only obliged to attend when invited but not as a routine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. And only for those issues that had to be dealt with together with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you wouldn't know -- let me actually re-start that question. Did you attend in May and June 1992 the weekly meetings of the corps commander's collegium?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in May and June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, while we're on this area of your statement, you mention in paragraph 65 that prior to the formation of the VRS and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, sorry, paragraph 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That prior to the formation of the VRS, Colonel Selak would go to Belgrade to brief General Vladan Sljivic, the commander of logistics of the JNA, and his superior. After the VRS was established, Colonel Selak, and then Colonel Skondric who succeeded him, would similarly brief General Djordje Djukic as to the functioning of the 14th Logistics Base in the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were mistaken when you read that he was subordinated to the JNA. When he went for briefings in Belgrade with General Sljivic, it is true that when he was commander of the 993rd Logistics Base he was directly subordinated to the assistant commander for logistics, and then when the 14th Logistics Base was set up it was part of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it is understood that as a commander he was duty-bound to report to the assistant commander for logistics of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to turn now to the supplies available to the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 09168.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, Colonel Selak was a Muslim and Colonel Skondric who succeeded him was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned Colonel Hasotic a moment ago. He was succeeded by Colonel Vukelic. Colonel Hasotic was a Muslim and Colonel Vukelic was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're asking me, I believe that that was the case but I'm not sure. But that -- because that happened while I was absent. I know about Hasotic and his duties in the 5th Corps, but I'm not sure what to say about what you are claiming. I believe that that was the case. Vukelic came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, Vukelic came right around the time that the 5th Corps transitioned to the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's on the record, which I'm not sure of, then I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave that topic and turn to this document. Now, we see here a report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff dated the 9th of October, 1992, reporting on the consumption of material in the 1st Krajina Corps between May and the beginning of October, 1992. Now directing your attention to the second point, we see total usage of ammunition, and we see immediately below that the 1st Krajina Corps had used about 3.350.000 from 7.62-millimetre automatic pistols during that period; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. But obviously this is for automatic rifles, 7.62. I can't read anything else. I can't interpret it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, shortly below that we see a note that almost 24 million rounds were used from a 7.62-millimetre automatic rifle; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen this before. I see it only now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 2 in the English and at the very bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S, under support ammunition, we see about 175.000 total mortar shells denoted with MB have been used by the 1st Krajina Corps during this period; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that. Please guide me to that part. I don't have the second page. I apologise. Mortars 82, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the bottom of the first page in the B/C/S. And let's take it step by step. I was adding the three numbers together, but we see --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you were adding things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see about 77.000 60-millimetre mortars have been used, about 93.000 82-millimetre mortars, and just over 10.000 120-millimetre mortars; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And now turning to page 3 in the B/C/S, staying on page 2 in the English. In the middle of the page in the B/C/S we see, combining the two different types of rockets, that about 1800 rockets have been fired during this period; right? By the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your calculation is good, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can I see the whole of the document? Can I see the signature as well? Show me the entire document including the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, there will be times when it's necessary to direct your attention but this is a pretty brief document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So if we could turn to the last page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what do I need to do? What am I supposed to do here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Here I'm simply showing you this is signed by Colonel Jankovic, the chief of the technical service; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I needed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 09168 receives exhibit number P6988, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, may I take it where the witness apparently says that he sees this document for the first time that -- I mean, for him to confirm that a document reads what it reads, we don't need a witness for that. This Chamber can read itself. Unless there's any follow-up which links the witness -- and you have not asked him whether this might be accurate numbers or not. You didn't ask anything apart from is this what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, I have just one more question about it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
