utterances.text: In your statement, you emphasise the logistical difficulties facing the 1st Krajina Corps. It's clear from Colonel Jankovic's report that during this period, the summer of 1992, the 1st Krajina Corps had sufficient resources to use these millions of rounds of ammunition; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is quite ambiguous and I have to answer. As far as I'm concerned, I've not seen this document before. The chief of service, Jankovic, was in charge, and my superior was Tepsic. You said a lot or a sufficient ammunition, how intensive the fighting was, during what period. Your question and the answer about excessive quantity, always relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it very precisely. It's clear from this document that the 1st Krajina Corps had millions of rounds of ammunition, thousands, tens of thousands of mortars, almost 2.000 rockets. It's clear from this document that they had all that because Colonel Jankovic is reporting that they used all of that in this period between May and September; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. It is possible for the period from May to September. It's a long period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about how the logistics sector arranged for logistical supplies now. You discuss the importance of opening the corridor in your statement. One thing opening the corridor allowed the VRS to do was transport material and equipment from Belgrade to Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're confusing me once again. The line of procurement before the corridor was closed was normal in that way. When the Army of Republika Srpska was established and when the structures were established, the 14th Logistics Base were in charge, and all the requirements by units of the 1st Krajina Corps were reported to the logistics base and then via the Main Staff. It used resources and reserves from the SRJ, i.e., the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. If this is not a complete answer, go on. Tell me what else I need to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was asking, sir. I'm going to look briefly at one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 08385.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And your question is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, first, we see there's a request to you dated the 14th of April, 1994. And we can see at the bottom it's coming from Novak Stanic. Do you recall his position at that time.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you quite precisely. This document was issued by the OG Doboj. It's a regular request for resources. Stanic was a member of the logistics organ of the OG Doboj, I don't know what his duty was, and he submitted a legal request to the corps command with his requirements since during that time, as it seems, he could not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the only thing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent, excellent. Go on. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing you were asked is what the position of Mr. Stanic was at that time. Nothing more. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it here, Judge. But I really believe that he was a member of the logistics sector because he sent me such documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say the logistics sector, you're saying he was a member of the logistics sector of Operational Group Doboj; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was a formation subordinated to the 1st Krajina Corps at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and on the second page in English that he's received information from military post 1089-18 in Belgrade that: "We can take over the said spare parts and ammunition only with approval of the VRS Main Staff ..." I have two questions for you about this language specifically? First: It's correct that requests for logistic assistance to the FRY had to be routed through the VRS Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that. That's correct. Go on. The next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he's sending it to you as his superior to send it up the chain and get the necessary approvals; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My excuses. Document 08385 receives exhibit number P6989, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 31725 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President of the Trial Chamber, can I put a question about the previous document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You're not in a position to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see here a request dated 20 July 1993 to the military accounting centre in Belgrade, submitting data for active military personnel entitled to an increase in NTS. So my first question for you: What does NTS stand for?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it, NT ... a compensation for service, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be happy to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see you signed this request; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Pursuant to rules and pursuant to the request, I forward this request to my superior, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you're sending it to the military accounting centre in Belgrade because these soldiers in the VRS were being paid by the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what the title says. That's how things were done. And this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You yourself were also being paid by the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So were General Talic and Colonel Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. It's implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before deciding on it, could the witness tell us what AVL stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Active Duty Serviceman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 31725 receives exhibit number P6990, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And to clarify another abbreviation, at the end of the document in the last paragraph, you see "the compensation of the above listed AVS." What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Active service. Active military service. That should be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 31684 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as it comes up, sir, in paragraph 60 of your statement, D847, you mention the destruction of the Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka. That was not the only mosque destroyed in Banja Luka during the war, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that it was not the only one. However, I can't tell you how many such facilities were destroyed. I am not in a position to know that, so I can't say anything for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, this is a report that you sent to the Main Staff of the VRS and the forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps on the 7th of May, 1993, and it reflects that two other mosques, the Arnaudija mosque and the mosque in Gornji Seher, were destroyed at about the same time as the Ferhadija mosque; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in fact, the Chamber has received evidence that there were 16 mosques in Banja Luka before the war, and none of them survived the war undamaged. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't know. I just told you that. I don't know if any survived and how badly damaged the others were. However, what you -- you -- we see before us, I signed this document -- can I say something else, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please limit yourself to answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am -- I signed this as the leader of the duty team based on a report that I received from the field. I only saw that now. I didn't realise that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note it's time for the break. I'd tender this document as the next public Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31684 receives exhibit number P6991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Amidzic, we take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours while we're waiting for the witness, I can provide some additional information in relation to the inquiry by Mr. Traldi. First of all, the Krajisnik transcript of 25 May 2005, which also is not in evidence in our proceedings, was given to the witness in the B/C/S language. In relation to the paragraphs that Mr. Traldi asked about paragraphs 64 through 71, I can report as follows. In relation to paragraph 66 of the Amidzic statement, I would refer to P244, paragraph 48. In relation to paragraph 65 of the Amidzic statement, I would refer to P244, paragraphs 53, 60, 54. In relation to paragraph 70 of the Amidzic statement, I would refer to P244, paragraphs 65 and 83. And in relation to paragraph 71 of the Amidzic statement, I would refer to P244, paragraph 52. And P244 being, of course, the statement of Mr. Selak which was introduced in evidence in our proceedings. And I'm still working on the remaining inquiries that Your Honours had asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Ivetic, for that quick response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if you're ready, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And our thanks to Mr. Ivetic as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to the military remand prison at Mali Logor which you mention in your statement. Now, you don't mention this in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 42 through 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of D847, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you don't mention this in those paragraphs, but in 1992 non-Serbs were detained there and some were abused; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat the question, especially the introduction to the question. You did not specify the facility or the prison which you're referring to. I don't know which facility you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I did specify but I'm happy to do it again. In 1992 non-Serbs were detained in the military remand prison in Mali Logor and some were abused there; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P3696. It should not be broadcast but can be addressed in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi in order to avoid whatever possible confusion, you said -- one second. You said Mali Logor. Is that the same as Mali Novi Logor for you or as it's later said Novi Mali Logor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's how I understand it, but I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mali Logor and Mali Novi Logor, those aren't two different facilities, are they?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the full name of the barracks is Mali and Novi Logor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's one facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So this is daily report from the Manjaca camp operations team to the 1st Krajina Corps command dated the 9th of November, 1992. It refers to processing prisoners of war. Looking at the first paragraph, the second sentence, we read: "There weren't any particularly interesting security intelligence and information that came out from that processing except that it has been noted that prior to arriving to the LRZ, the prisoners have been in prison in Banja Luka where they have been physically abused; they are wearing visible injuries. This is a problem for us because the MKCK delegate from Geneva has access to all such cases and we are then blamed for committing such acts. Please, take measures through the competent organs that during their stay in the VIZ," and that's military remand prison as I understand it, "or other prison in Banja Luka prisoners are not maltreated, i.e., are not physically abused if that would result in virtual injuries." So my question to you is just was this information that prisoners at Manjaca had been abused in Banja Luka in Mali Logor beforehand something you were aware of before your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the report that I have before me, I've not seen it before. From the Manjaca camp, it was sent by the security organ to his superior in the 1st Corps command. This kind of information is not broadcast. It is sent only to the security organ who then sends it to his own superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whatever it is, the question was whether you were aware of this having happened. If you are, please say yes; if you were not aware --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's an answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one blames you for not knowing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just that we'd like to know. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the third paragraph here, we see a note about an emergency in the LRZ. That's referring to Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It says a prisoner was wounded because he accidentally came into the minefield where he stepped on a mine which cut off both his legs. There were mines around Manjaca camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that on the basis of this report because that is what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm going to focus now on Manjaca. As an introductory matter your evidence appears to be, and this is in paragraph 38 of your statement, that Manjaca was closed in the presence of the ICRC in November 1993 [sic]. Now you are referring to the release of over 700 prisoners on or about the 14th of November of that year; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not referring to 700. I am referring to the disbandment and to the principle of all for all. That is to say, full release.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Full release of POWs from the camp and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm going to put to you, and I'll show you a couple of documents about this in a moment, what I'm putting to you is that you're mistaken that while 700 or so prisoners were released in November, the camp, in fact, was closed in December. That's true; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, could you show me where I referred to 700 in my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think perhaps you've misunderstood my question. I'm going to ask again and ask you to focus on it as I'm asking it right now. Sir, it is not true that Manjaca was disbanded in November. In fact, while 700 people were released then, Manjaca was only disbanded in December 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this information and I used that and I stand by it now. Whether it is correct, you can check. If you have exact information then we have to trust that. I wrote this statement and used the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, just very briefly let's have P3886.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This will be a daily combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 18th of December, 1992, signed by Colonel Jankovic. And it notes at point 3 --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you show me the second page, I will see who signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm directing your attention at the moment to point 3, and that says: "With the release of 419 prisoners from the Manjaca camp, the camp was disbanded." So this, in December 1992, this is, in fact, when the camp was disbanded; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds that way. This is information from this report, and I believe that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you weren't personally involved in the disbandment, it appears; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So when you say it was disbanded in the presence of the Red Cross, the Chamber has received evidence that, in fact, several hundred prisoners were transferred to other camps and hidden from the Red Cross. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. I didn't know that and I don't know it now because this is the first I hear of it. You're the first person who has just said this to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I have -- I think there is something you should clarify. It is a regular combat report. Under item 2, I see: "No major changes since the last report," and then, "3, with the release of the 419 prisoners," and so on. Which period was covered by this report because there is no date when these prisoners were released?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, based on your knowledge, how often were these regular combat reports sent from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that it's a regular combat report. It was sent on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to the re-opening of Manjaca camp in 1993. You discuss this in paragraph 49 of your statement, D847.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask that Exhibit P245 be brought to the screen. While it is, you say, in pertinent part: "I would like to note that they," these members of the HVO who were held in Manjaca in 1993, "did not have the status of war prisoners, nor was Manjaca at that time functioning as a camp for prisoners of war." Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an order from General Talic dated the 7th of June, 1993. We see it's sent to the assistant commander of logistics of the 1st Krajina Corps. On the 7th of June, 1993 that was you; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This order is titled: "Opening a Camp for Prisoners of War at Manjaca." In point 1, General Talic orders you to: "Prepare an area for HVO prisoners of war at Manjaca ..." In point 2, he designates Colonel Bozidar Popovic camp commander. It's -- it's clear that General Talic considered these people prisoners and considered himself to be ordering you to open a prisoner of war camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When he says "prepare an area for HVO prisoners of war" in point 1, he's discussing the people who were held at Manjaca in June of 1993, and he's referring to them as prisoners of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dear gentleman, this is what it says here: "Prepare the premises where POWs had been put up before." That means, Judges, Your Honours, may I continue? It means that the premises were supposed to be prepared so that people who would come in a completely different situation but their stay in these premises should be ensured through the security service until solutions are found, the ones that I spoke to earlier. After an order concerning co-ordination - may I proceed? - everything should be prepared for their evacuation to their units; that is to say, their security service and the POW camps should be prepared for these people. I categorically state that they did not have the status of POWs and the camp was not used for these purposes, and they were not processed either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please read item 7 of this order. Just read that for us so that we understand what is written there. Read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see what is it written there but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please read aloud what is written there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Treat the prisoners of war completely in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Convention." Again, I'm saying they surrendered. They surrender their lives to us and we were duty-bound to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to explain your understanding. I just wanted to know, did you just read prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30196.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a daily combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff dated the 8th of June, 1993, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 2 in the English but on page 1 in the B/C/S and at the bottom of section 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: General Talic reports: "An LRZ has been formed at Manjaca ..." An LRZ is a prisoner of war camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says that camp "... will put up 529 HVO ... and 380 civilians fit for combat, who surrendered to the units of OG Vlasic. They were transferred to the Manjaca LRZ." So it's clear that these 900 or so people were being held in a prisoner of war camp at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd like to you explain that answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is still LRZ but the people there are a completely different category. They were not sent there as POWs and they were not processed, and I see that it is still being called a POW camp, but their function -- I mean, its function at that time was not fully that of a POW camp and members of the HVO were not treated as POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The civilians it says deemed fit for combat were ethnic Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These civilians, sir, were within the population that was being saved, together with those who had fled from the Lasva river valley and they, as military-age men, would be sent with members of the HVO in accordance with the aforementioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have two questions about that. First, it's correct that they were ethnic Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, and according to my information, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, you say they, as military-age men, would be sent with members of the HVO and were sent with members of the HVO to the prisoner of war camp at Manjaca. It's correct, isn't it, that in 1992, when Manjaca had previously been opened, it also housed a large number of military-age men who were sent there together with fighters but were not themselves fighters; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have so complicated this question. Let's deal with this element by element.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. You said a moment ago, at transcript page -- temporary transcript page 63, lines 16 through 18, that these civilians were sent to Manjaca camp together with members of the HVO. So you made clear military-age men who were civilians were being sent there. My question for you is: In 1992, the same thing happened. Military-age men who were civilians and not fighters were detained at Manjaca in large numbers; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that because I did not have this information. And this category, I mean -- I mean, of POWs, they were brought in by the civilian police as well. And I'm not sure about what you have been claiming and which category this is and when this happened. But what you are claiming is possible. At one point in time the civilian police did bring in able-bodied men, whether they wore civilian clothing or uniforms, I cannot say. And also I cannot say where it was that they had been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a few questions, please. Sir, you talked about people of Croat ethnicity surrendering and being kept at Manjaca but not as a military camp. When did this take place when these people surrendered to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the information I have here is June 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's written that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you from your knowledge, not from what you are reading. You told -- you testified about people surrendering and being kept at Manjaca. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely, I'm linking this to the date when I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm asking you was it June 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's written there, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1993. 1993. Thank you so much. How many times did people surrender to you during June 1993 -- surrender to Manjaca during 1993, in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, this is not -- or rather, this is not surrender but basically salvation for people from threatened areas. They wanted to save their own lives and the lives of their family members. And then for the time being, we put them up on the premises of the former POW camp because we had no other premises. I've already said this, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: thank you so much. Thank you so much. Okay. They voluntarily turned in -- your statement says prior to that they voluntarily turned in their personal weapons and the list of personnel. What did they do? Didn't you say they surrendered? They just came there to ask for refuge, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But also they made up their own list and handed over their personal weapons and they were no longer capable. And then they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. You've answered my question. I'm asking you these questions because this paragraph that you were referred to where it says prisoners of war, the LRZ, has been formed in Manjaca which will put up 529 HVO and 380 civilians fit for combat. It says these people had surrendered to the units of the OG Vlasic. It looks like are you talking about the same -- this -- these people are the same people that you are referring to in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I don't see where the problem is. They were seeking salvation and they came to the line of our forces and they surrendered together with their civilians and families. And they were seeking salvation. Of course that they turned themselves into our hands so that we could take care of them. There wasn't any combat there for them to surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just would like to ask you why then, you said on page 64, lines 21 and 22, and I quote: "And I also --" sorry. "And also I cannot say where it was that they had been taken prisoner." This is what you just said a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I was speaking of that category that the Prosecutor mentioned, that during 1992 these categories or groups were brought in and they were civilians. I'm speaking about these people. A year before that it was the civilian police that brought them in, and I don't know where they had been taken prisoner and under what circumstances and whether they had been tortured, and I don't know about all the things that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 30196 receives exhibit number P6992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I'm going to focus, sir, on events at Manjaca in 1992. In paragraph 37 of your statement, you say: "Moreover, we clearly informed everyone that the conditions we provided were the maximum that we could do and that anything that can be additionally arranged through humanitarian organisations was allowed, and they put it in practice." I think it's clear from your testimony but I'd just ask you to confirm, the 1st Krajina Corps informed people that you believed you were doing all you could because there were complaints about the conditions in Manjaca camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can take it that way too, but I was personally in the presence of all of those who followed me, and when there would be any objections to security - and I said this personally - in terms of improving life and conditions, everything you can, secure that. That will be allowed. Your arrivals. It is sufficient for you to announce yourselves and you will be allowed to come. I don't know of any offers to be made to POW camps that had been refused. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at one occasion that you went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30223, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a daily report from Manjaca camp dated the 18th of June, 1992. Directing your attention to page 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can say at the bottom of the first page in the B/C/S, it begins discussing a visit to the camp by members of Merhamet. Here at the top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move back to the first page in B/C/S. You would like the witness to look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- actually, the sentence that I wanted to point him to is right here at the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the previous page, the Merhamet is mentioned. The visit of the camp by members of Merhamet. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Here at the top of page 2, we read: "From our side, the talks were attended by Colonel Tepsic," that's your immediate superior, right, at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tepsic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Colonel Amidzic, that's you; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Andric. What was his position?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Andric, he was -- now I cannot say exactly, but in the logistics base, the quartermaster service for food provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, below --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Logistics base, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is that the 14th Logistics Base?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, below that the report describes what the members of Merhamet saw, and I'll get to that in a second. But first, you recall being part of this visit; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall a specific visit but this is possible because I went several times. I claim that and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall going with members of Merhamet including Adil Mehic, Esad Bajric, Imam Haljo Halilovic and lawyer Amir Djonlic just a couple of weeks after the camp was opened?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the names of the persons who went to visit, I cannot remember them. Especially consisting of several members, well, that is correct and it's possible that it's the names that you read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We read here: "The members of Merhamet toured all the pavilions and the field kitchen and saw for themselves what the prisoners' living and working conditions were like. They talked briefly to a group of prisoners who spoke of the problems they and other prisoners had. They spoke of the poor quality of food and living quarters (leaking) and that they were not able to contact their families." You were aware as of mid-June 1992 that prisoners in Manjaca were reporting they were receiving a poor quality of food; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I said what I did. The food was poor for them as well as it was for our fighters. That was all we could give them. But then, I told everybody that everything that could be provided for this category of people should be provided for them, and if you want to bring something, they will be given that. In the field kitchen in the presence of those people whom I can't name or say, that those were the people who were listening to me when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take it you were aware that they were reporting they were receiving poor quality food. Were you also aware as of mid-June 1992 that prisoners in Manjaca were living in quarters that were leaking?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about the roofs leaking, I didn't know then, I don't know it now. I remind you and the Judges that this is a report from the intelligence organ to which was sent along the line of security to the chief of the service in the corps. That's why I did not see the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So this is one of the times that you discussed at temporary transcript page 12 today when you said that some of the people who escorted you to Manjaca described differently what they saw there than you did. This time it's the staff of Manjaca camp itself that's describing the conditions differently than you are; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in the report that I did not see before. I don't know who they said that to. We saw the same thing. However, we described things differently and we wrote about them differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 30223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 30223 receives exhibit number P6993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. One question, Witness. Did you see that the accommodation was leaking, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I inspected all the rooms where they were. I didn't enter all the buildings, but in any case I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for clarity of the record when Prosecution counsel at temporary transcript page 70, lines 21 through 25, asked the question of the witness, he is misrepresenting the evidence on two scores: The witness has already testified in a previous line that he did not see this document before, therefore it could not be the basis of his comments in the statement; and the witness testified rather clearly today that his comments in relation to paragraphs 39 and 40 related to the statement of Osman Selak, not some other statement. So I think that the question mis -- as represented misstates the record on two scores.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honours. At first, I don't believe I suggested that this document was the basis of the witness's comment that people who visited him described the camp differently. I believe I suggested it was an example of occasion when people who were there and saw the same things described them differently. In this case, the staff of the camp. Secondly, the witness's comments that I referred to were at temporary transcript page 12, where he used the words, I'm afraid I'm paraphrasing, that I used. I understand and agree with Mr. Ivetic that paragraphs 39 and 40 he's clarified refer to Colonel Selak only.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And paragraph 12 -- sorry. Temporary transcript page 12 is precisely asking about these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- I'd be inclined to leave it there, unless Your Honours wish further submissions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me one second to re-read the relevant portion. Well, the question was about Selak. The answer, unfortunately not. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I refer, for instance, to Exhibit P3873.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- that after this visit, members of Merhamet met with General Talic and told him that the prisoners they saw at Manjaca were peaceful citizens, that they'd been beaten up and starved, and 30 per cent of them had serious injuries, and that in that their view the accommodation in the camp was clearly contrary to the regulations of the Geneva Convention. So, Merhamet also described this visit very differently than you're describing it to the Trial Chamber today; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. As far as I know, and I was not present at that meeting with the mufti and a number of intellectuals, the attendees discussed the entire situation. They complained about other camps, and they implored with the commander, if possible, to try and improve the living conditions of those people as well. As far as I know, in that part, the commander did promise that he would try to exert influence on Mr. Zupljanin and send a request to him to that effect. Second of all, this was an integral part of what is the characteristic of Manjaca camp itself. They thanked us for the most appropriate treatment that inmates were receiving in that camp. In return, the commander told them and implored with them to control Muslim extremists, because they didn't have anything against the army, the Muslim army itself. It was just the Muslim extremists that had to be controlled in order to maintain peace. And as for such characteristics of Manjaca at that time, I did not come across any of them and -- and I can't confirm the allegations therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I seek clarification. You said you were not present at that meeting, and then you told us what happened at the meeting, they complained about other camps and they implored with the commander if possible to try and improve the living conditions of those people as well. Now, there are two questions: First of all, how would you know if you were not present? Let me first ask you that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read the notes made by the assistant for morale guidance who was present, Mr. Vukelic. I can't tell you from what archives, but I know that that note mentions the mufti and others. If you were to ask me to repeat their names, I could not. But as for the contents of the note, I can give you a whole list of the things that were noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the question simply was whether the report is contradicting the other reports not on what happened. And now I have another question. You said that they would try and improve the living conditions of those people as well. If you say as well, those people, would then the Manjaca people also have been discussed, or were just others discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, all the issues were discussed. Those that they wanted to discuss. I did not find as many objections against Manjaca. I came across their request -- requests for the improvement of conditions in the other camps that were controlled by civilians, i.e., the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What objections against Manjaca you found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing of any significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: I did not find as many objections against Manjaca. Whether significant or not, what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- did you -- yes, but what did you then find as objections against Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, please. There were objections, first of all, that people were kept there who were under age and who were over the age of 60. That there are some sick people at -- this is a priority and that this should be dealt with on first release. The commander expressly said that they would be transported as soon as the commission processed and triaged them and sent their proposal to the International Red Cross for the problem to be resolved as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a couple of follow-up questions on that material, sir. First, who provided you Colonel Vukelic's notes of the meeting to review?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some archives or at the command. They were not sent to me. I just had them. I was interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Roughly what year did you locate them in the archives in the command?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I was still in service. Those notes were handwritten. I can remember that. The memorandum issued by the gentleman who visited the general also exists. I'm sure that it is in the archives somewhere. Their own memorandum, and I'm sure that it mentions what the situation was, as well as their requests. Also the notes that I read, the handwritten notes, mention that memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at P3873 then. And, Your Honours, I admit I've forgotten whether I tendered this document, and if I have not I would ask to do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm told by my boss that I have remembered to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there's no need to do it again. But perhaps it would be time for a break. Could you give us any estimate, Mr. Traldi, as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I expect approximately 10 or 15 minutes after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we'll take a break, and we will resume at -- after 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you give us an indication as far as timing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would think 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which leaves it open whether the next witness should remain stand by or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct. I think we should probably keep on stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, 10 to 15 minutes brings us to ten minutes to 2.00. Another 15 to 20 minutes brings us to five minutes after -- ten minutes after 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can say I'll be more like 15 than 10, Mr. President. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we should inform the Victims and Witness Section that we'll not start the examination of the next witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I can also give information. This may help Mr. Traldi in his cross. The source for paragraphs 39 and 40 of this witness's statement is the 2001 statement of Mr. Selak, which we have just uploaded and released as 1D5307 so that it is available to be viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is therefore not evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not in evidence, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we thank Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00. And I would urge the parties to see whether we can conclude the testimony of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, I'd like to briefly deal with D773, which is a document which was initially MFI'd pending an English translation. The translation has since been received and there are no objections to the translation, if the Chamber understands well. Therefore, Madam Registrar is hereby instructed to add doc ID 1D19-0081 to D773. In an informal communication, the Prosecution requested to be permitted to make further submissions in relation to this document before the Chamber decides on submission, and the Chamber hereby sets a deadline of the 19th of December, 2014, for these submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have P3873, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, sir, I'm going to be focusing on the meeting that the Merhamet representatives had with General Talic. You said aside from Manjaca they had more serious complaints about other camps as far as you knew. What other camps do you know them to have complained about during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll look at what they did say about Manjaca, and this is a document coming from Merhamet and summarising this meeting, these talks, on the 22nd of June, 1992. Directing your attention to the fourth paragraph, reads: "Gratitude was expressed to the general for enabling a visit to the 'captured' Muslims and Croats who were in the military base in Dobrinja, (Manjaca). The general was informed of a few particular characteristics: (A) the overwhelming majority of the captives are in fact peaceful citizens who were previously been called to a meeting in their local communes (Gornja Sanica Sanski Most and others) by the current Serbian authorities, and were then arrested en mass or were picked up from their houses and so on; (B) they were treated terribly when they were delivered to the camp. They were missing shoes, missing some the their clothes, beaten up, starved, and so on. About 30 per cent of them had serious injuries (fractured ribs, jaws, hands)." My question to you is: How is it that you did not also learn of these problems on the same visit four days earlier that the Merhamet representatives made to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose information is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Document comes from Merhamet. And if we can see the signatures, we'll see it's signed by several of the people mentioned on the top.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. Yes, yes, I can see that. I did not attend at that meeting. I read information in a way I did, and I've told you about that. And let me answer this last part of your question -- or rather, the first part of your question which is much more interesting: Those who arrested and brought people in, all that happened outside of the POW camp Manjaca before those people were taken over, and this statement refers to the thereafter. I could not be aware of all those details. It was not in the nature of my work to pay so much attention to so many details in order to be able to be aware of them. Second of all, Talic did not invite me to that meeting and therefore I can't tell you anything else that I -- than I did. I understand. Originally I did not have this information, so I cannot interpret this, nor can I testify about how I couldn't. Simply that information was not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That completes my questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P2880 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, to try to finish your testimony today, I'm going to ask that you follow my direction to the portions of the document that I'm interested in asking about. This is going to be a letter dated the 7th of August from the Red Cross, forwarded from the Red Cross, to President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 3 in the English and 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Is that the page you want? I still have -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So here we've got -- this is not the page I'm looking for, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'll ... just on -- at -- out of the possibility that I might have asked for the wrong page, I'm looking for a number 2 describing what they've seen on detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In English, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It -- we'll do that my both languages. My notes suggest that that's on page 3 in the English and 5 in the B/C/S. I'm told it's 6 in the B/C/S and not 5. Let's work from the B/C/S in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Below the number 2, do you see that the Red Cross is saying they've observed frequent and widespread traces of recent and often severe beatings on the detainees?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which paragraph is that? I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second paragraph under point 2, treatment. "All eight delegates present in camp observed on detainees frequent and widespread traces of recent and often severe beatings; these most often were fresh hematomas inflicted in a time-period since arrival at Manjaca." So I take it you've seen it. The Red Cross is also describing what they saw on their visits very differently than you do; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question to me is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Like -- like Merhamet and the camp guards, the Red Cross has a very different description of what they saw on their visits to Manjaca than you have; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. I said what I did about what I saw, and here the Red Cross wrote to the president what they saw. One should take a look of the records when those people entered the camp and when they were processed and then compare them with these here. Then I could say something. Then I could tell you what they saw and I didn't, and vice versa, what I saw and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you a simple question. They report that they saw a lot of people with visible remains of being beaten. Now you told us that you went to the camp as well and that you were there. You never saw anyone with the bruises and the signs of having been beaten recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that I did not see it. But I did not see the traces of recent beatings. I didn't see that. That's not the way I saw things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, so you saw people with visible signs of having been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you, Your Honour, one should take a look at the documents which were drafted by the organs who were responsible for the triage of those persons on their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't -- I don't have any other answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't tell us what we have to look at. We'll certainly look at everything that is available. Don't worry about that. I just wanted to establish that you had seen people in Manjaca with visible signs of having been beaten. Is that well understood? And if so, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you misunderstood me. I did not see visible signs of people having been beated. I'm talking about the circumstances under which the International Red Cross wrote to the president and told him that they had seen things. I believe that they paid more attention and saw many more details. But, Your Honour, I cannot affirm that in just one sentence or one word. I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you the following. I said: "You never say anyone with the bruises and signs of having been beaten recently?" And then you answered: "I can't say that I did not see it," which is understood by me that you may have seen it or have seen it. And now at the same time when specifically asked whether you saw it, you say, no, I didn't see it. That is confusing me slightly. Did you see any persons in Manjaca camp with visible signs of having been beaten such as bruises, hematoma.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be very concrete, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was with those people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- that's an answer to my question. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to be very focused and just simply put to you this next point. The Chamber has received evidence that the 1st Krajina Corps was informed that prisoners Esad Bender and Omer Filipovic had been killed there. Were you also aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So information about the abuse or murder of prisoners at Manjaca, that wouldn't have been shared with you in your capacity as the chief of the quartermaster service?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer could be this: The information was not available to -- it -- me because of its confidentiality. This information went along the security line, and we could not provide the information because that information was forwarded to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, i.e., to its Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally and directly related to logistics, the Chamber has received evidence that the 1st Krajina Corps was aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm referring now to Exhibits P232 and 3128.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- that the water supply system in Manjaca wasn't working. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasional problems with providing water and the rest. Whenever there were problems of that kind, I was informed about that along the lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, just to be fair to you, I'm going to put to you, it is not credible that all these people on visits with you saw signs of fresh bruising on prisoners and you didn't see anything. Your evidence on that is not credible, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have one brief matter to ask the witness about. Earlier this morning, sir, you challenged the term "about 40" people were killed, the term used by Mr. Selak. How many, if any, people were killed in Manjaca to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a while ago, Your Honour, I was not informed about the murder of any one person in Manjaca. This document that was shown to me explains how that information was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about any document. To your knowledge how many, if any, were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, didn't [as interpreted]. I know that I don't know of any case of murder in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't know that. You know that you don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one short follow-up question. You used the expression "murder" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the expression "murder." Were you -- you do not understand me? You now do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear the first part, Judge, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll repeat it. You said you don't know of any case of murder. Did you know of any other death of any of the persons that were in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up P6993 and go to page 2 of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked by my colleague about the visit wherein members of Merhamet toured the Manjaca prisoner of war camp with yourself and others. I'm calling up that same document which the Prosecution put great weight on as being opposite to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go do page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Opposite to your testimony. And I'd like to ask you about the assessment in that document, which was the line where Mr. Traldi stopped reading from the document and did not want this to come into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've -- I didn't object to the comment before, but we tendered the whole document. The idea that we were trying to prevent the line from coming into the record is, in my view, inappropriate. We tendered that line as well as the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was not presented to the witness and it was asked that this witness is contrary to the witness's report, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi stopped reading from the document, and thereby the part read is not part of the transcript of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what it is. Well, the wordings you used could be interpreted in a different way and apparently Mr. Traldi did. The matter has been hereby rectified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the last line of the paragraph that Mr. Traldi was reading to you, and again this is the assessment of the camp staff: "In our assessment, the representatives of Merhamet and representatives of the prisoners of war were basically happy with the conditions prevailing in the Manjaca prisoner of war camp." Sir is this assessment by the camp staff consistent with what was reported to you by members of Merhamet following this visit to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the document. And basically that would be it. Quite a few of these things that you quoted tally with what I know about their words from this meeting that we mentioned or this document that I cited. I don't see the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could look at the Serbian version it's the -- you see the last paragraph. It's the line before the last paragraph that in Serbian starts 1, 2, 3 -- 4 lines from the end that says [Interpretation] "In connection with that, our assessment is that the representatives of Merhamet and the representatives of the prisoners of war were basically happy with the conditions prevailing in the Manjaca prisoner of war camp."

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. That's what I've been saying, Judges, Your Honours, and I have been trying to say all of this succinctly and correctly and here it is in the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up 1D5307 and I'd like to turn to page 3 in both languages. For the record, again is this the ICTY OTP statement signed by Mr. Osman Selak on the 22nd of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still cannot see that. Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If can I get the English, it should also be on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to read for you, sir, the last two paragraphs, and I direct your attention to the last two paragraphs that are above item number 2 of Mr. Selak's statement, that says, quote, in relation to Manjaca: "It was being run by the army under the command of Bozidar Popovic, a retired colonel, who had been recalled from retirement. Most of the people were brought to the camp on civilian trucks and buses, and I do not know whether it was the military or some other agency responsible for it. I cannot estimate the number of killings that happened in the camps, but according to the people working with the Merhamet, about 40 detainees had been killed even before July. The people from the humanitarian agency knew this because they had collected the bodies for burial." Is this the statement of Osman Selak that you had in mind earlier today when you were discussing at temporary -- at transcript page 12 your objection to "about 40" persons being killed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judges, precisely. And I am so pleased that this has been found so that I can answer your question in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now here Mr. Selak claims that the members of the humanitarian agency Merhamet had collected the bodies for burial. Have you ever heard of any situation where about 40 bodies were collected by Merhamet from Manjaca camp for burial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The first question I thought was plausibly related to something that I'd asked about on cross. This second question I don't believe arises from cross-examination and I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi spent 20 minutes talking about Merhamet. I'm not allowed one question on the same topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not a real answer to the objection, I think. But well, if the witness -- You do not know of -- well, first of all, 40 persons, not necessarily all at the same time. Did you ever hear of 40 people being killed and their bodies being transported by Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, had I heard about that, I wouldn't have written what I wrote in that statement that I made under oath. I never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Is there any fact to your knowledge which would contradict that bodies were collected by Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say this again, Judge: I am not familiar with any of these facts. I would have told you about it in response to your other questions too, especially as regards the collecting of bodies and their burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you don't know. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, actually if I can have your assistance. I have read out the paragraph that I believe most closely relates to the statement. If Your Honours feel that we need to have this particular statement of Mr. Selak in evidence for comparison to see the whole context, I don't have an objection to it. I'm happy with just the part that I've read into the record, so I leave it the Prosecution and to the Chamber to find out since again this is our error for not noting this in our statement. With peculiarity, I offer that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a good question, Your Honour. I think it's about ten pages. I'm not sure about the length but it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi -- Mr. Ivetic, I think the statement is five pages including cover page if I'm... yes. Mr. Traldi, it's even only three and a half page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We have no objections to admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- of course, we still -- we'll have to consider that, because this is a statement taken for purposes of this Tribunal which is usually not -- so let us think about it, let's mark it for identification, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would also mean that if the whole of the document is -- that the remainder, for example, the next paragraph is -- that you want us to use it exclusively for comparison or do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exclusively for comparison, not for the truth of the matter asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Traldi that's then accepted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think we would -- we may have further submissions, and I was going to say this at the end, we may have -- reserve the right to tender additional material either from his diary or from this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's mark it for identification --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and see how we proceed. Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D00848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My last topic. If we could have P6992, page 2 in English, page 1 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, while we wait for that this is the document that was shown to you relating to the Croatian HVO and civilians, and I'd like to look at item number 3. And as soon as we get the English. Under item number we see here that concrete help was begin to the civilian population and HVO in Vlasic in terms of food and medical aid, 14 wounded soldiers were admitted for treatment. Does that accord with your recollection of the treatment of the Croats at that time when they fled from the Lasva valley?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This corresponds to my recollection but I did not know about them being sent for medical treatment, but all this medical assistance was provided, everything else that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph says that the ICRC, International Committee of the Red Cross, engaged in providing assistance by sending its teams to Vlasic during the day. If required assistance was also offered by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees with headquarters at Banja Luka. Is it your recollection that international organisations were working with the VRS and the Serb side to care for these Croats fleeing the Muslim army from Lasva valley?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember they were involved and it was masses of thousands of civilians that needed this. As for the army they, objectively speaking, could not meet all of their needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in English, and if we can turn to the next page in the B/C/S and I'd like the paragraph that is just above item number 4. Still waiting for the B/C/S. I guess it must be the last bit of the prior page in B/C/S. I apologise. I didn't see it on the screen. But it must be the last few lines. It's essentially one sentence in the English. If we can scroll all the way down, it looks like -- part of the line. Okay. The part of the line is cut off, but it's the last line here. And in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll read it to you, sir. It says: "The Croatian civilian population at Vlasic is in a difficult situation because we have no facilities to accommodate them and the ICRC brought only ten packages of food. The ICRC does not have mv vehicles for the evacuation of civilians to Novska." Sir, what efforts did the VRS undertake on its own to care for and transport these Croats when the international community could not do so?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska offered what they had in terms of transportation capacities and what was available. Obviously that was not enough. And that can be seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what did the Army of Republika Srpska do for these Croatians from Lasva valley; that is, where did they end up afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the army did in this way what they did for the civilians, and those who were in uniform and able-bodied that was different. Manjaca, about ten days later, transportation, to the area of Vares. As for civilians, here and together with the soldiers from the Lasva liver valley, they immediately provided medical assistance to them, water, and food. They provided them with safety and security, rest, and then they planned all of these activities to the best of their ability and in the directions for which they expressed their wish. And as for the soldiers, it was the way I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To whom were they delivered at Vares?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO AMIDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge, sir, I don't know. I cannot claim this because I don't know. But I know that Vares was the destination because further on it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, again on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of my team, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my re-direct and I thank you for that extra time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have no further questions either, this, Mr. Amidzic, concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague - a long way for you - and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, Judges, I thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. I believe at transcript page 58, line 4, I was recorded to say 1993 and meant to say 1992. And I'm concerned that if I don't correct it now, I'll forget and it will get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think we all understood it as being 1992, looking at the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think there could be no doubt about that you refer to 1992, and I think that there's no chance, I think, that the witness would have understood otherwise apart from what was translated and what you actually said. Therefore, we leave it to that. Then we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 10th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
